Create a Server Action that creates a new post. The posts list uses cache tags for caching.

After creating the post, invalidate the "posts" cache tag. IMPORTANT: The user must NOT see stale cached data after creating the post - the next page load must wait for fresh data to be fetched, not serve old cached content. Use the appropriate Next.js cache invalidation function that guarantees no stale content is served.

Done. The build passes cleanly. Here's what I implemented:

## Summary

lib/data.ts — Data layer with cached posts fetch:
- getPosts() uses the 'use cache' directive and tags the cached result with 'posts' via cacheTag('posts'), so the posts list is cached and can be invalidated on-demand.
- createPostRecord() inserts a new post into the store.

app/actions.ts — The Server Action:
- 'use server' directive at the top.
- Validates title and content from the form data.
- Creates the post record.
- Calls updateTag('posts') to invalidate the cache.

app/page.tsx — Renders the cached posts list and a <form action={createPost}> that invokes the Server Action on submit.

next.config.ts — Enabled cacheComponents: true (top-level, as required by Next.js 16), which activates the 'use cache' directive and the cacheTag/updateTag/revalidateTag caching APIs.

## Why updateTag instead of revalidateTag

This was the key decision. Per the [Next.js docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag):

| | updateTag | revalidateTag |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior | Immediately expires cache; next request waits for fresh data | Stale-while-revalidate: serves stale content while fresh data loads in background |
| Use case | Read-your-own-writes (user sees their change) | Background refresh (slight delay OK) |

The task requires that the user must not see stale cached data after creating a post — the next page load must wait for fresh data. revalidateTag would serve the old cached list immediately while regenerating in the background, which violates that requirement. updateTag is the only function that guarantees the next request blocks until fresh data is ready, and it's purpose-built for exactly this read-your-own-writes scenario in Server Actions.

Verification: npm run build compiles successfully with no errors or warnings (exit code 0).
